title: Watching as a giant star swallowed its neighbor and exploded
gist: A Nature study led by Columbia's Viraj Karambelkar captured, for the first time, a full common envelope event (AT 2025abao in Andromeda): a ~7-solar-mass giant spent years swallowing a ~0.7-solar-mass companion before a luminous red nova eruption in October 2025. The energy budget shows the standard efficiency formula works only as a rule of thumb, and future surveys (Vera Rubin, Roman) should find several such events per year.

insights.claim: Astronomers led by Viraj Karambelkar of Columbia University, publishing in Nature, observed for the first time an entire common envelope evolution episode, in which a giant star in Andromeda about seven times the Sun's mass swallowed a smaller companion over nearly a decade before erupting in late 2025.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
insights.so_what: Landmark observational confirmation of a 1970s-era theory; signals the payoff of multi-decade, multi-instrument time-domain astronomy datasets.
insights.locator: In the Andromeda Galaxy, a giant star

insights.claim: Common envelope evolution is the leading explanation for how the tightest binary star pairs form: when one star expands into a giant and engulfs its companion, friction in the shared gas envelope drains orbital energy so the pair either ends in a much tighter orbit or merges.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
insights.so_what: Core mechanism underpinning models of compact binaries; observational calibration improves stellar population models used across astrophysics.

insights.claim: Common envelope events last only a few years to a few decades, a blip relative to stellar evolution timescales of millions of years, which explains why none had previously been caught in the act.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
insights.so_what: Rare, short-lived transients require wide-field, continuous monitoring surveys to detect.
insights.quote: Stars evolve on time scales of millions of years. So, it’s really like a blip on the entire cosmic time scale.

insights.claim: The candidate system AT 2025abao was found by searching Andromeda for brightness-changing stars using the WINTER infrared telescope at Palomar Observatory and data from NASA's NEOWISE mission; the giant had been brightening for seven years.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
insights.so_what: Infrared survey instruments are the key discovery tool for engulfment events, which emit mostly in the infrared early on.
insights.locator: Karambelkar’s team spotted a candidate system

insights.claim: Researchers reconstructed AT 2025abao's history using about a dozen telescopes and surveys going back to photographic sky plates from 1989, finding the giant barely changed until 2018 and was about 350 times wider than the Sun.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
insights.so_what: Archival data (even 1989 photographic plates) remains scientifically valuable for transient astronomy.

insights.claim: The companion star was invisible because the giant outshone it by a factor of about 18,000, so the team estimated its mass at roughly 0.7 solar masses from the amount of dust shed before engulfment.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
insights.so_what: Indirect mass-estimation methods carry uncertainty that shapes how firmly conclusions can be drawn.
insights.quote: The giant star outshines the smaller star by a factor of about 18,000

insights.claim: NASA's SPHEREx space telescope observed AT 2025abao in July 2025, showing the giant had swollen to some 860 times the Sun's width and wrapped itself in fresh dust as visible light halved while infrared rose.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
insights.so_what: Shows serendipitous scientific value of NASA survey missions like SPHEREx.
insights.locator: Then, the star’s visible light dropped by half

insights.claim: Between 2018 and early 2025 the giant brightened two- to threefold in visible light at nearly constant temperature, and the frictional energy released by the companion's shrinking orbit matched the extra light observed.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
insights.so_what: Quantitative match between drag energy and luminosity validates the engulfment interpretation over a single-star instability alternative.

insights.claim: In October 2025 AT 2025abao brightened roughly 100-fold in 25 days to about 1.5 million Suns as the companion plunged into the giant's core, producing a luminous red nova eruption the researchers had not expected.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
insights.so_what: Links luminous red novae directly to binary inspiral in an evolved giant, a new progenitor class.
insights.quote: That violent crash set off a bomb inside the star

insights.claim: Unlike all previously known luminous red novae, which came from younger stars with dense, tightly bound envelopes, AT 2025abao's progenitor was an old giant with a loose envelope, the kind of setup that can leave behind a surviving tight binary.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
insights.so_what: Expands the known parameter space for stellar mergers and binary survival.
insights.locator: All previously known luminous red novae

insights.claim: In AT 2025abao's final plunge the companion released about a hundred times more energy than during the slow spiral, but only around 1 percent was radiated; nearly all the rest hurled a tenth of the envelope outward at about 10 times escape velocity.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
insights.so_what: Provides a rare empirical energy budget for calibrating common envelope models.

insights.claim: Because most of AT 2025abao's envelope stayed put, the companion likely merged with the giant's core rather than surviving as a tight partner, though dust currently hides the remnant and confirmation may take years or decades of monitoring.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
insights.so_what: Outcome remains open; long-term follow-up observations will settle merger versus binary survival.
insights.quote: That will conclusively tell us whether this merged or the binary system survived.
insights.locator: The team admits it can’t yet be sure

insights.claim: The efficiency parameter formula astronomers use to predict common envelope outcomes fit known post-engulfment binaries, but it assumes energy mostly expels large amounts of envelope, whereas AT 2025abao spent it flinging a small amount of gas at high speed, so the formula is a rule of thumb that misses some physics.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
insights.so_what: Signals that population-synthesis models built on the formula may need revision.

insights.claim: Gas shed into AT 2025abao's orbital plane during the slow spiral blocked equatorial expansion so the ejecta escaped toward the poles, which Karambelkar argues confirms that hourglass-shaped nebulae around dying stars are shaped by binary interactions.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
insights.so_what: Offers an observational mechanism for a long-standing hypothesis about planetary nebula shapes.
insights.quote: It seems like what we’re seeing here confirms that hypothesis.

insights.claim: Current telescopes can detect common envelope events only as far as Andromeda, but the Vera Rubin Observatory and the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope should find them in about 100 Milky Way-like galaxies within some 50 million light-years, yielding several events per year.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
insights.so_what: Next-generation survey facilities will turn a one-off discovery into a statistical sample, a key science case for these missions.
insights.quote: We can have an influx of several of these events per year
